landing:
My p5 Pet

Make a creature that reacts to you. Its body, home and personality are yours to choose.

Start by running your pet. Then choose any part below.

Give it controls

  • Click your pet — Choose where a click counts.
  • Press a key — Give the keyboard a job.

Give it a body

  • Shape a body — Round, wide, tall or something else.
  • Make an angular body — Try a robot, rock or boxy beast.
  • Add decorations — A hat, spots, whiskers or wings.

Make it move

  • Wobble from side to side — Make a slow sway or an excited wiggle.
  • Bounce up and down — A gentle bob or a big bounce.
  • Follow the pointer — Make a curious companion.

Give it personality

  • Switch between moods — Give an action a reaction.
  • Surprise me — Make the next reaction unpredictable.
  • Give it a voice — Use words to show its personality.

Make its home

  • Draw a place to live — A garden, bedroom, cave or planet.
  • Invent a strange world — Underwater, in space or somewhere new.

Test and improve

  • Meet test and change — Watch someone play and improve one thing.

Ideas to borrow

  • A curious companion — A pet that follows you around.
  • A sleepy oddball — A pet with very little energy.
  • A space visitor — A creature from somewhere else.

1A.title: Meet your pet
1A.html:
Meet your pet

Your starter pet already has a body, a home and a reaction. Get it working, then change any part.

Open your workspace

  • Open the Raspberry Pi Python editor in another tab.
  • Copy the pet starter below. Replace everything in main.py with it.
  • Select Run. A purple pet should appear in the visual output.
Copy the pet starter
python
from p5 import *

# Your pet's starting point
x = 200
y = 230
mood = 'calm'
message = 'Click my body!'


def setup():
    size(400, 400)
    no_stroke()


def draw_home():
    background('lightblue')
    fill('lightgreen')
    rect(0, 290, 400, 110)


def move_pet():
    pass  # Your pet can stay still for now


def draw_body():
    fill('orchid')
    ellipse(x, y, 110, 100)


def draw_face():
    fill('white')
    circle(x - 20, y - 15, 24)
    circle(x + 20, y - 15, 24)
    fill('black')
    circle(x - 20, y - 15, 10)
    circle(x + 20, y - 15, 10)
    if mood == 'happy':
        ellipse(x, y + 20, 30, 20)
    elif mood == 'sleepy':
        ellipse(x, y + 20, 12, 20)
    else:
        ellipse(x, y + 20, 24, 5)


def draw_accessories():
    pass  # Add decorations here when you want them


def react():
    global mood, message
    if mood == 'calm':
        mood = 'happy'
        message = 'Hello, friend!'
    else:
        mood = 'calm'
        message = 'That tickles.'


def mouse_pressed():
    if dist(mouse_x, mouse_y, x, y) < 60:
        react()


def key_pressed():
    pass  # You can give a key a job later


def draw():
    draw_home()
    move_pet()
    draw_body()
    draw_face()
    draw_accessories()
    fill('black')
    text_size(18)
    text(message, 20, 365)


run()

Open the starter file if you prefer to copy it from a file.

Test

Click the middle of your pet. Its mouth and message should change. Click again to change them back.

You have made your first working pet!

Keep your code

Use the editor's Download button to keep a copy of your Python project. If you log in, you can also save it in the editor.

This pathway saves your ticks and notes separately. Save notes does not save your Python code.

Choose your next part

Start with controls, a body, movement, personality or a home. You can come back and change things.

How to use the code on these pages
  • A function is a named chunk of code with one job.
  • When a page says replace a function, replace its line starting with def and all the indented lines below it. Stop before the next def.
  • Keep one copy of each function. Two versions with the same name do not run together.
  • Keep run() at the very bottom. Keep the four spaces at the start of lines inside a function.
  • Combine ideas from different parts. Options that replace the same function are alternatives; adapt one to include your own changes.
My pet did not appear
  • Check you copied the whole starter, including its first and last lines.
  • Look for an error message. Check the line it mentions for a missing bracket or changed spaces.
  • If the editor says Load failed, refresh it or return to its home page and choose Python.

Choose a part.

2A.title: Click your pet
2A.html:
Click your pet

A click can be a pat, a tickle or a surprise. You decide what it means.

Before you test

Have you run your starter? That is the only step you need first.

Try the code

Replace mouse_pressed(). The distance check makes clicks near the centre of your pet count.

python
def mouse_pressed():
    if dist(mouse_x, mouse_y, x, y) < 60:
        react()

Test

Run your code. Click your pet, then a far corner. Only the click near your pet should change its face and message.

Make it yours

Change 60 to make the touch area bigger or smaller. To accept a click anywhere, remove the if line and move react() left by four spaces.

Choose another part.

3A.title: Shape a body
3A.html:
Shape a body

Build a creature from a few shapes. It does not have to be an animal anyone has seen before.

Before you test

Have you run your starter? That is the only step you need first.

Try the code

Replace draw_body(). The ears are drawn first so the body sits in front of them. The face is drawn separately.

python
def draw_body():
    fill('orchid')
    ellipse(x - 35, y - 45, 25, 65)
    ellipse(x + 35, y - 45, 25, 65)
    ellipse(x, y, 110, 100)

Test

Run your code and click your pet. Your new body should still have a face that reacts.

Make it yours

Try wide ears, tiny ears or no ears. An ellipse uses centre x, centre y, width and height. Keep positions relative to x and y so every part moves together.

Choose another part.

3B.title: Make an angular body
3B.html:
Make an angular body

Circles are only one possibility. Try building with rectangles and triangles.

Before you test

Have you run your starter? That is the only step you need first.

Try the code

Replace draw_body(). A rectangle uses its top-left corner, then width and height.

python
def draw_body():
    fill('gold')
    rect(x - 50, y - 45, 100, 90)
    fill('orange')
    triangle(x - 25, y - 45, x, y - 75, x + 25, y - 45)
    rect(x - 65, y - 10, 15, 35)
    rect(x + 50, y - 10, 15, 35)

Test

Run your code. Click the middle of the body to check the reaction still works.

Make it yours

Change the top into a horn, aerial or mountain peak. Keep your face visible. If you make a much bigger body, adjust its clickable area in Click your pet.

4A.title: Wobble from side to side
4A.html:
Wobble from side to side

Repeated movement can give even a simple shape a personality.

Before you test

Have you run your starter? That is the only step you need first.

Try the code

Replace move_pet(). The sine function makes a smooth repeating wave; you can explore the numbers without learning the maths first.

python
def move_pet():
    from math import sin
    global x, y
    x = 200 + sin(frame_count * 0.04) * 75
    y = 230

Test

Run your code. Watch the pet move left and right. Click its body while it moves to check it still reacts.

Make it yours

Change 0.04 for the speed and 75 for the distance. Try small changes first. Keep your pet inside the canvas.

Choose another part.

4B.title: Bounce up and down
4B.html:
Bounce up and down

Make a pet that cannot keep still.

Before you test

Have you run your starter? That is the only step you need first.

Try the code

Replace move_pet(). The absolute value keeps each bounce above the starting height.

python
def move_pet():
    from math import sin
    global x, y
    x = 200
    y = 230 - abs(sin(frame_count * 0.05)) * 80

Test

Run your code. The pet should rise and return to the same place. Its face and decorations should travel with it.

Make it yours

Change 80 to set the height and 0.05 to set the speed. Could it float gently instead of bouncing?

Choose another part.

4C.title: Follow the pointer
4C.html:
Follow the pointer

Where you move, your pet follows.

Before you test

Have you run your starter? That is the only step you need first.

Try the code

Replace move_pet(). The limits keep the centre away from the edges.

python
def move_pet():
    global x, y
    x = max(70, min(330, mouse_x))
    y = max(100, min(270, mouse_y))

Test

Run your code. Move your pointer around the visual output and into each corner. The pet should follow and stop near the edges.

Make it yours

Make a pet that only follows sideways by replacing the last line with y = 230. On a touchscreen, try dragging a finger across the canvas.

Choose another part.

5A.title: Switch between moods
5A.html:
Switch between moods

Your starter already connects a click to a reaction. Now decide what that reaction means.

Before you test

Have you run your starter? That is the only step you need first.

Try the code

Replace react(). Both your click control and any keyboard control call this same function.

python
def react():
    global mood, message
    if mood == 'calm':
        mood = 'happy'
        message = 'You found my tickle spot!'
    else:
        mood = 'calm'
        message = 'Again?'

Test

Run your code and use your control twice. The face and message should swap each time. Your body and home should stay as you designed them.

Make it yours

Rewrite both messages. Try sleepy instead of happy: the starter already knows how to draw that mouth. Your rule is: When someone ___, my pet ___.

Choose another part.

5B.title: Surprise me
5B.html:
Surprise me

Perhaps your pet has a mind of its own.

Before you test

Have you run your starter? That is the only step you need first.

Try the code

Replace react(). A random choice picks one mood whenever you use a control.

python
def react():
    from random import choice
    global mood, message
    mood = choice(['calm', 'happy', 'sleepy'])
    if mood == 'happy':
        message = 'Play time!'
    elif mood == 'sleepy':
        message = 'Five more minutes...'
    else:
        message = 'Just watching.'

Test

Run your code. Use your control several times. You might get the same mood twice; that is allowed by a random choice.

Make it yours

Change the messages. Repeat happy in the list to make it more likely. If you invent a new mood, add a matching rule to draw_face().

Choose another part.

5C.title: Give it a voice
5C.html:
Give it a voice

A message can make the same creature seem shy, dramatic or very silly.

Before you test

Have you run your starter? That is the only step you need first.

Try the code

Replace react(). This pet chooses a new line each time. Its voice is written on screen.

python
def react():
    from random import choice
    global mood, message
    mood = 'happy'
    message = choice([
        'Is that a biscuit?',
        'I meant to do that.',
        'More adventures, please!'
    ])

Test

Run your code and use your control. Check every message is short enough to fit inside the canvas.

Make it yours

Write three lines for your own pet. Keep them short. You could borrow the strange food ideas from Python Bytes.

Draw a place to live

Make somewhere your pet belongs. The starter pet can stay still while you work on its home.

def draw_home():
    background('skyblue')
    fill('gold')
    circle(330, 65, 65)
    fill('white')
    ellipse(95, 70, 100, 35)
    fill('lightgreen')
    rect(0, 290, 400, 110)
    fill('seagreen')
    triangle(15, 290, 65, 180, 115, 290)

Test

Run your code. Your pet should appear in front of the scenery. Check its message is still easy to read.

Make it yours

Turn the sun into a moon, the tree into a mountain, or the ground into water. The canvas runs from 0 to 400 across and down.

7A.title: Meet test and change
7A.html:
Meet test and change

A pet that reacts to you is a finished first version. What would make yours more fun?

Test

  • Let someone meet your pet. Can they work out how to interact?
  • Try each control. Does the pet react as you intended?
  • If it moves, try the edges. Do its face and decorations stay attached?
  • Can you read every message?

Change one thing

Ask: What surprised you? What would you try next? Pick one change, edit your code, then test again.

Something broke when I combined ideas
  • Keep just one definition of each function. A later copy replaces the earlier one.
  • Keep your starter's draw() function: it runs each part in order.
  • If part of the face stays behind, use positions based on x and y.
  • If a control does nothing, check it calls react().
  • Undo your last change and run again. Bring it back a little at a time.
